title: Present perfect: ever, never, just, already, yet
tagline: A past action that still matters now — have/has + the third form of the verb.
why: Has your class finished the project? Have you ever tried ceviche? The present perfect connects the past to now — a completed action with a present result, or an experience at some point in your life without saying exactly when. At A2 Key it turns up in short emails (I've already bought the tickets) and in questions like Have you ever been to…?

hook.text: At the market, Miss Vega checks the shopping list. "Have you found the mangoes, Nadia?" "Yes, I've already found them!" "And the bread, Mateo?" "I haven't bought it yet."
hook.ask: The present perfect always has two words together: have/has + a past participle (like found or bought). Can you find all three pairs in the story?

diagrams.title: A past action that connects to now

marks.label: the mangoes are in the bag now

diagrams.caption: Present perfect links a past action to now — we don't say exactly when it happened.

diagrams.title: Build the sentence in the present perfect
diagrams.caption: The little words already, yet and ever move around the sentence, but they always sit next to have/has or the participle.

diagrams.title: been vs gone

rows.label: Meaning
cells: went there and is still there (or on the way)

rows.label: Example
cells: She has been to Cusco. (she's back now)
She has gone to Cusco. (she's there now)

rows.label: Use it for
cells: life experiences — Have you ever been to…?

diagrams.caption: Same participle idea, opposite result: been = there and back; gone = there and still away.

use.point: have/has + past participle — regular and irregular
ever and never — experiences in your life, no exact time

examples.note: ever in questions = at any time in your life
never = at no time, always with a positive verb

examples.text: She's the best cook I've ever met!

use.point: just, already, yet — very close to now

examples.note: just = a moment ago, between have and the participle

examples.text: We've already paid for the mangoes.
examples.note: already = sooner than expected, between have and the participle
yet = up to now, at the end of a negative
yet also goes at the end of a question

use.point: been vs gone, negatives and questions

examples.text: She's been to the market — she's home now.
He's gone to the market — he isn't here.
examples.note: gone = went and is still there

watch_out.why: The past participle of see is seen, not see — have/has always needs the third form of the verb.

watch_out.wrong: I have finished my homework yesterday.
watch_out.why: Yesterday is a finished time word — it needs the past simple, not the present perfect.

watch_out.wrong: She has already went to the shop.
watch_out.right: She has already gone to the shop.
watch_out.why: After have/has, use the participle (gone), not the past simple form (went).
Never usually goes between have/has and the participle, not before have.

watch_out.wrong: Have you ever went to the beach?
watch_out.right: Have you ever been to the beach?
watch_out.why: After have, use been, not went — went is only for the past simple.

l1.why: The verb after have/has must be the participle (eaten), not the base form.
For a life experience with no exact time, English prefers the present perfect — Spanish often just uses the simple past for both ideas.
Never sits after have/has, between the helper and the participle, not before it.
The participle of finish is finished (regular -ed) — don't drop the ending after have.

l1.wrong: She has been to the market.
l1.why: Gone means she is still there; been means she went and came back — the two are opposites in English.

remember.trick: have/has + 3rd form = the past that matters NOW.
remember.tip: Think of it as a link: something happened, and it's still important right now — that's why have/has never lets go of now.

dialogue.title: Shopping at the market
dialogue.context: Saturday morning at the market in Lima. Miss Vega and the class are buying food for the school picnic.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Yes, I've already found them — they're in the bag.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Great. Mateo, have you bought the bread yet?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Not yet. I haven't gone to that stall.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I've just bought some avocados — look, three for one sol!

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: He's gone to buy water. He isn't back yet.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: OK. Have you two ever tried a lucuma?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: No, I've never tried one! Is it good?

can_do: I can talk about life experiences with have/has + past participle and ever/never.
I can use just, already and yet to say how recent or how complete something is.
I can tell the difference between been and gone.
summary: Present perfect = have/has + past participle. It connects a past action to now, without saying exactly when.
Ever and never talk about experiences in your whole life; just, already and yet talk about something very close to now.
Been = went there and came back; gone = went there and is still away.
Finished-time words like yesterday and last week need the past simple, not the present perfect.
Negative: haven't/hasn't + participle. Question: Have/Has + person + participle.
